terms.definition: An element that is dull, often brittle, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity.
terms.function: Fills the upper right of the periodic table and includes the gases of the air we breathe.
terms.whereItIs: The upper-right region of the periodic table.
terms.whyItMatters: Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, and the other life-critical elements are nonmetals.

terms.definition: A quality of some solids — they shatter when struck instead of bending.
terms.function: Shows one of the sharpest differences from metals, which bend and hammer flat.
terms.whereItIs: The sulfur lump in the model, which splits under the mallet.
terms.whyItMatters: Brittleness is a quick physical test for telling a nonmetal solid from a metal.

terms.definition: A bond formed when atoms share electrons with each other.
terms.function: Holds nonmetal atoms together in molecules like O₂, CO₂, and water.
terms.whereItIs: Between the atoms inside every molecule of a nonmetal compound.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the main way nonmetals connect — and the foundation of organic and biological chemistry.

terms.definition: A member of the nonmetal family in Group 17, like fluorine and chlorine.
terms.function: Shows that even within the nonmetals there are families with shared behavior.
terms.whereItIs: The second-from-last column of the periodic table.
terms.whyItMatters: Halogens connect the nonmetal family to reactivity and everyday compounds like table salt.
